Hugo Usage Guide Applies to Hugo v0.168.0 (Extended). Commands use the macOS/Linux shell as examples. Compiled from the official Hugo documentation. Theme-specific private configuration should follow the actual theme repository.
1. Installation and Version Check macOS (Homebrew):
brew install hugo hugo version hugo env On Linux, use the corresponding distribution package or the binary officially released by Hugo. When using SCSS/Sass or certain theme asset pipelines, confirm that the installed version includes the Extended feature.
2. Creating a Project hugo new project myblog cd myblog git init Typical directory structure:
myblog/ ├── archetypes/ # Templates for new articles ├── assets/ # Assets that need to go through the resource pipeline ├── content/ # Markdown content ├── data/ # Data files ├── i18n/ # Theme interface translations ├── layouts/ # Custom templates, can override theme templates ├── static/ # Copied as-is to the site root ├── themes/ # Local themes or Git submodules ├── hugo.toml # Site configuration (YAML and other formats are also supported) └── public/ # Build output (generated after running hugo) Hugo itself does not include a complete blog appearance. If there is no available theme or custom layout, you may see a warning such as found no layout file for "html".
3. Using a Ready-Made Theme (Git Submodule) The following uses the Ananke theme from Hugo’s official quick start as an example:
git submodule add https://github.com/gohugo-ananke/ananke themes/ananke Configure in hugo.toml (do not declare the same TOML key twice):
baseURL = 'https://example.com/' title = 'My Blog' theme = 'ananke' Start the preview:
hugo server -D Different themes vary in menus, homepage, parameters, Hugo version, and asset compilation dependencies. When migrating configuration, prefer the theme’s README and example site. Do not copy another theme’s [params] block as-is.
Git Submodule Maintenance Cloning on a new machine:
git clone --recurse-submodules <repository URL> Filling in submodules for an existing clone:
git submodule sync --recursive git submodule update --init --recursive Updating submodules (will track the configured remote branch; review changes before committing):
git submodule update --remote --merge git diff --submodule git add .gitmodules themes/ git commit -m 'Update Hugo theme' When migrating a submodule’s Git URL: first modify url in .gitmodules, then run git submodule sync --recursive. If the CI network is unstable, you may switch to an accessible Git mirror, but make sure the mirror has the required commit objects; you may also initialize submodules yourself after cloning the main repository.
4. Creating and Editing Articles hugo new content posts/hello-world.md Example article:
--- title: "Hello World" date: 2026-10-17T12:00:00+08:00 draft: false description: "Article summary" tags: ["Hugo", "Blog"] categories: ["Tech"] --- This is the body. ## First-level section **Bold**, *italic*, [external link](https://gohugo.io). Key fields:
Field Purpose title Title date Article time draft true means draft, not included in the default production build description Summary, whether to display it depends on the theme tags, categories Taxonomy, specific page display depends on the theme slug Custom URL tail segment (the actual path is also affected by the permalink configuration) Note: articles with a future date may also be excluded from the default production build; check the date, time zone, and --buildFuture.
Images and Static Files Site-wide static files go in static/images/logo.png, referenced in articles as:
![Logo](/images/logo.png) A page bundle can use:
content/posts/hello/ ├── index.md └── cover.jpg Write ![Cover](cover.jpg) in index.md. If you want to use theme image processing, thumbnails, and other features, you still need to follow the page-resource conventions of that theme.
5. Local Development and Build hugo server # Preview published content hugo server -D # Include drafts hugo server --bind 0.0.0.0 # Allow other devices to connect; mind network access controls hugo # Output to public/ hugo --gc --minify # Common production build hugo -d dist # Output to dist/ Hugo’s build command does not automatically clear the output directory before building. If you delete articles, change URLs, or switch languages, old files may remain. It is recommended to clear the artifacts in the CI’s temporary build directory before building, rather than blindly cleaning any path.
rm -rf public hugo --gc --minify Only run the above deletion when you have confirmed that public/ is purely a build artifact with no user data.
6. Multilingual Sites The following shows the basic configuration for Chinese and English. The supported language menu and switcher depend on the theme:
baseURL = 'https://example.com/' title = 'My Blog' defaultContentLanguage = 'zh-cn' defaultContentLanguageInSubdir = false [languages] [languages.zh-cn] languageName = 'Simplified Chinese' languageCode = 'zh-CN' weight = 1 title = '我的博客' [languages.en] languageName = 'English' languageCode = 'en-US' weight = 2 title = 'My Blog' One way to organize content by language directory:
content/ ├── zh-cn/ │ └── posts/hello.md └── en/ └── posts/hello.md Before using the above language directory layout, combine the multilingual content directory configuration or language mounts to confirm that content is correctly attributed. A simpler approach that needs no extra mounts is using translation filenames in the same directory, such as hello.zh-cn.md and hello.en.md; the default language’s URL can also be arranged per the project configuration.
Recommendation: for sites that already have content/posts/, start with the filename suffix method:
content/posts/ ├── hello.zh-cn.md └── hello.en.md It is best to set a consistent translationKey on translated pages (only needed when the file path cannot directly associate them), to avoid the multilingual menu pointing to the wrong page.
7. Using HTML in Markdown Hugo uses Goldmark by default. If you see Raw HTML omitted while rendering in the log, raw HTML in Markdown is not being rendered. Only enable this in hugo.toml when you trust the article content:
[markup.goldmark.renderer] unsafe = true Once enabled, embedded HTML in articles will participate in the output. If the content comes from untrusted contributors, consider the risk of script injection.
8. Git and Gitea Actions Publishing It is recommended to keep the source repository (including .gitmodules, content/, hugo.toml, etc.) separate from the static publishing repository or branch. A typical CI flow:
push to source main │ ▼ Pull source and theme submodules │ ▼ Install the specified Hugo version │ ▼ Clean the temporary build output and run hugo --gc --minify │ ▼ Commit the public/ files to the publishing repository's main or publishing branch │ ▼ Caddy / Nginx serves the static directory You can first verify these commands inside the build container:
git submodule sync --recursive git submodule update --init --recursive rm -rf public hugo --gc --minify find public -maxdepth 2 -type f | head Gitea Actions example workflows must be configured individually based on the act_runner’s labels, container image, Git authentication, permissions, Hugo install path, and target branch. Do not assume GITHUB_SHA or custom COMMIT_SHA automatically exists in every shell step; with set -u, undefined variables will cause the build to fail directly. To get the source commit value, run inside an already-checked-out Git repository:
SOURCE_SHA="$(git rev-parse HEAD)" Use a separate working directory for the target publishing repository, to avoid accidentally deleting source files. Check for non-fast-forward conflicts on the branch before pushing. Do not use unchecked git push --force as a general publishing strategy.
9. Common Troubleshooting 9.1 found no layout file for "html" The cause is usually that the theme was not loaded correctly, the theme is missing the corresponding template, or the theme name in the config file does not match the themes/ directory.
ls -la themes/ cat .gitmodules hugo config | grep -i theme hugo --logLevel debug Confirm that template files such as layouts/ actually exist inside the theme directory, and check the theme’s own usage notes. Do not silence a blank-site warning.
9.2 Raw HTML omitted Check markup.goldmark.renderer.unsafe as in Section 7. You can also try to replace raw HTML with Markdown or Hugo shortcodes.
9.3 Git Submodule Directory Is Empty git submodule status --recursive git submodule update --init --recursive If a network error is reported, check the URL, authentication, and DNS/proxy inside the build container in .gitmodules, not only the host network.
9.4 Page Not Published Check the article’s draft, date, expiration time, language, and the target theme’s routing. Check:
hugo list all hugo list drafts hugo list future hugo list published 9.5 CI Build Succeeds But Published Content Does Not Change Check whether public/ contains the expected HTML, whether the publishing branch was updated, whether the web root points to the latest deployment location, and whether the browser/CDN is caching old content. Do not assume it is a Hugo caching problem first.
10. Recommended Daily Workflow # 1. Pull updates (including submodules) git pull --ff-only git submodule update --init --recursive # 2. Create a new article hugo new content posts/new-post.md # 3. Edit and preview locally hugo server -D # 4. Change draft to false in the article's front matter # 5. Commit and push (CI builds/publishes automatically) git add content/ git commit -m 'Add new post' git push 11. References Hugo Official Documentation Quick Start Command Line Reference Basic Usage Markdown Rendering Configuration Hugo Modules

On an Armbian machine used as a bypass router, both sing-box and WireGuard are running side by side. The router itself resolves internal domain names fine, yet downstream clients that point at it as their DNS server time out every time. The root cause turned out not to be the DNS matching rules, but rather that the traffic sing-box sends to its upstream DNS was choosing the wrong egress interface.
All addresses in this article are rewritten illustrative values, not the original network configuration; the topology relationships and protocol behavior of the private network are preserved.
Topology and Symptoms Role Illustrative Address Purpose Downstream client 192.168.10.20 DNS client Bypass router LAN 192.168.10.254 / eth0 Address where sing-box DNS listens Bypass router WireGuard 10.77.0.11 / wg0 Tunnel client Internal DNS 10.77.0.1:53 DNS server on the WireGuard peer The topology looks like this:
Client 192.168.10.20 │ DNS query ▼ Bypass router 192.168.10.254:53 (sing-box DNS inbound) │ Expected: query 10.77.0.1:53 out through wg0 ▼ WireGuard peer DNS 10.77.0.1:53 The internal test domain used is service.home.arpa (illustrative). The observed symptoms:
The router itself resolves that domain normally; When a downstream client explicitly sets the router’s LAN IP as its DNS server, queries time out consistently; sing-box is listening on UDP 53, and the corresponding inbound routing rules have been confirmed correct. Step 1: Confirm the Inbound Request Arrives Capture the downstream client’s DNS traffic on the bypass router:
sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -nn -K -l \ 'host 192.168.10.20 and udp port 53' You will see requests carrying the same DNS Transaction ID retrying every few seconds, with no matching successful response. This tells you the client did hand the query to the router, but the processing chain never completed.
Check the listening port:
sudo ss -lnup | grep ':53 ' This confirms sing-box is listening on UDP 53 at the bypass router’s LAN IP.
Step 2: Observe the LAN and WireGuard Egresses Separately Don’t start by dumping all DNS traffic. Open two terminals and watch each path separately:
# LAN: only this downstream client sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -nn -K -l 'host 192.168.10.20 and udp port 53' # WireGuard: only the target DNS server sudo tcpdump -i wg0 -nn -K -l 'host 10.77.0.1 and udp port 53' Then issue one explicit query from the downstream client:
nslookup -type=A service.home.arpa 192.168.10.254 What turned up in this case: the downstream request did arrive on the LAN, but sing-box’s new queries to the DNS upstream left from eth0 with the LAN address as the source, instead of leaving from wg0 with the WireGuard IP.
Key distinction: a DNS rule that “picks a particular upstream server” and the OS/application decision of “which interface to use to reach that server” are two separate things. Even when the rule matches correctly, the request can still time out if the actual egress path is wrong.
Step 3: Bind an Interface for the sing-box DNS Upstream The upstream configuration at the time of the failure looked like this:
{ "type": "udp", "tag": "internal-dns", "server": "10.77.0.1" } After the fix:
{ "type": "udp", "tag": "internal-dns", "server": "10.77.0.1", "bind_interface": "wg0" } bind_interface applies to the network dial for that DNS server, making it use the specified interface. In an environment with TUN, policy routing, and WireGuard, this is more explicit than relying on the system’s automatic path selection.
Check the configuration and restart the service (adjust the path to your own configuration file):
sudo sing-box check -c /etc/sing-box/config.json sudo systemctl restart sing-box Then query again and capture on wg0:
sudo tcpdump -i wg0 -nn -K -l 'host 10.77.0.1 and udp port 53' You should see the request on wg0 along with its matching response. In this case, adding bind_interface restored normal downstream DNS resolution.
Side Observation: NXDOMAIN After a Successful A Record During the investigation, another class of symptom came up: an internal name resolves through a CNAME to a single-label hostname, the A query returns an address normally, but a subsequent AAAA query for the final hostname returns NXDOMAIN. This is a separate resolution anomaly that still needs its own investigation — it should not be mistaken for the cause of the downstream query timeouts.
If you see something similar, run these separately:
dig @<DNS server address> service.home.arpa A dig @<DNS server address> service.home.arpa AAAA And check whether the CNAME points at an unexpected single-label name, and whether the local resolver and the upstream DNS return consistent results.
Troubleshooting Takeaways Capture packets segment by segment along the chain: client → bypass router inbound → upstream egress → upstream response → client response. Verify the actual egress interface and source IP of the packets; the server field in the DNS configuration alone tells you nothing. When you receive the client’s request but see no matching response, check the upstream egress first; there is no need to immediately modify routing rules that have already been verified as correct. If tcpdump reports bad udp cksum, it may be the result of NIC checksum offload on locally sent packets; -K disables checksum verification during capture. home.arpa is a special-purpose domain for home networks; do not publish real public domain names, device names, internal addresses, and tunnel topologies as-is on a public blog. Conclusion: the final failure point was that sing-box’s upstream UDP queries to the internal DNS were leaving through the LAN interface instead of going over WireGuard. Setting bind_interface: "wg0" on the corresponding DNS upstream server fixed it.
summary: On an Armbian machine used as a bypass router, both sing-box and WireGuard are running side by side. The router itself resolves internal domain names fine, yet downstream clients that point at it as their DNS server time out every time. The root cause turned out not to be the DNS matching rules, but rather that the traffic sing-box sends to its upstream DNS was choosing the wrong egress interface.
title: Troubleshooting DNS Timeouts on a Bypass Router: sing-box Upstream Queries Leave Through the Wrong Network Interface

After deploying sing-box TUN on Armbian, I encountered a rather counterintuitive issue: IPv6 ping works, but IPv6 HTTPS connections time out after enabling auto_redirect.
The eventual finding was that the problem was not with IPv6 public routing or the proxy node, but rather that the Linux loopback interface lo was missing the ::1/128 address. This article documents the diagnostic process and the fix.
Environment Linux: Armbian, ARM64, 6.18-series kernel sing-box: 1.14.x Network management: Netplan + NetworkManager Transparent proxy: TUN, auto_route: true, auto_redirect: true IPv6: Automatically configured by the upstream; the interface already has a global IPv6 address and an RA default route To protect privacy, this article omits the actual public IP addresses, MAC addresses, router address, domain names, and custom internal routing table numbers. The ULA addresses and test targets in the following examples are for demonstration purposes.
Symptoms Direct IPv6 HTTPS test:
curl --noproxy '*' -6 -v --connect-timeout 5 \ --resolve 'cloudflare.com:443:[2606:4700::6810:85e5]' \ https://cloudflare.com/ After enabling sing-box:
* Trying [2606:4700::6810:85e5]:443... * Connection timed out after 5002 milliseconds curl: (28) Connection timed out Comparison test:
State IPv6 HTTPS sing-box stopped Normal auto_redirect: true Times out auto_redirect: false Normal However, a simple ping -6 test may succeed. ICMP connectivity cannot substitute for a TCP/HTTPS test.
Troubleshooting Process 1. Rule Out Issues with the IPv6 Address and Default Route ip -6 addr show dev eth0 scope global ip -6 route show default The interface already has a global IPv6 address, and the default route was learned through RA, in a form such as:
default via fe80::... dev eth0 proto ra When NetworkManager manages IPv6, whether RA is functioning correctly should not be determined solely from the value of net.ipv6.conf.eth0.accept_ra; the actual addresses and routes must also be observed.
2. Find That TCP Does Not Appear Directly on tun0 or eth0 Observe the HTTPS target through packet capture:
sudo tcpdump -ni tun0 'ip6 and tcp port 443' sudo tcpdump -ni eth0 'ip6 and tcp port 443' With auto_redirect enabled, the expected TCP SYN to the target IPv6 address was not observed. This does not necessarily indicate packet loss: sing-box’s nftables rules may first redirect the TCP traffic to a local port.
3. Inspect the Local REDIRECT in nftables sudo nft -a list table inet sing-box The rules contain content similar to the following:
meta l4proto tcp ... queue flags bypass to 100 meta l4proto tcp ... redirect to :23457 return The port shown here is an internal listening port used in this troubleshooting environment; other versions or configurations may use different ports. Check the IPv6 listener:
sudo ss -6 -lntp '( sport = :23457 )' sing-box is indeed listening on that port.
Continue capturing traffic on the loopback interface:
sudo tcpdump -ni lo -vv 'tcp port 23457' The key packets observed at this point are similar to the following:
IP6 2001:db8::1234.4210 > ::1.23457: Flags [S] IP6 2001:db8::1234.4210 > ::1.23457: Flags [S] IP6 2001:db8::1234.4210 > ::1.23457: Flags [S] The 2001:db8::/32 prefix above is a documentation-only example IPv6 prefix, not an actual public address.
The SYN packets are continually retransmitted without a SYN-ACK, indicating that the connection has been redirected to the local ::1 address, but the local TCP handshake cannot complete.
4. Identify the Root Cause: The Loopback Interface Is Missing an IPv6 Address ip -6 addr show dev lo The output is unexpectedly empty. Normally, the loopback interface should have the following:
inet6 ::1/128 scope host Because ::1/128 is missing, an IPv6 TCP REDIRECT to the local ::1 address cannot establish a connection normally. This matches the repeated SYN packets and the absence of a SYN-ACK.
Fix First, inspect the IPv6 state of lo:
ip link show lo sysctl net.ipv6.conf.lo.disable_ipv6 ip -6 addr show dev lo If IPv6 is disabled:
sudo sysctl -w net.ipv6.conf.lo.disable_ipv6=0 Ensure that the loopback interface is enabled:
sudo ip link set lo up If ::1/128 still does not appear, add it manually:
sudo ip -6 addr add ::1/128 dev lo Verify:
ip -6 addr show dev lo ping -6 -c 2 ::1 curl --noproxy '*' -6 --connect-timeout 5 https://api6.ipify.org The issue can only be considered resolved after confirming that HTTPS also works when auto_redirect: true.
If the problem occurs after a reboot, check whether /etc/sysctl.d/ contains a configuration that disables IPv6 on lo. You can explicitly set the following in the sysctl configuration file:
net.ipv6.conf.lo.disable_ipv6 = 0 Note that this setting only ensures that IPv6 is not disabled on lo; it does not automatically guarantee that ::1/128 will always exist. If the address disappears again after a reboot, continue investigating the startup order or the service managing lo.
Summary A successful IPv6 ping does not mean that IPv6 TCP proxying is working; a real HTTPS request must be used for verification. After enabling sing-box auto_redirect, some TCP traffic is redirected by nftables to a local port; capturing only eth0 or tun0 may not reveal the expected target traffic. Confirming the listener with ss and observing SYN retransmissions with tcpdump -i lo were key to identifying the problem. The final point of failure was the absence of the IPv6 loopback address ::1/128 on lo. Temporarily disabling auto_redirect works around the problem, but fixing the loopback interface is the actual solution for this failure. Quick Diagnostic Command Reference ip -6 addr show dev lo sysctl net.ipv6.conf.lo.disable_ipv6 ip -6 route show default sudo nft -a list table inet sing-box sudo ss -6 -lntp '( sport = :23457 )' sudo tcpdump -ni lo 'tcp port 23457' Addendum: Downstream Devices Cannot Access the Network After Enabling UFW After resolving the IPv6 loopback issue, I enabled UFW on Armbian and encountered another phenomenon: the Armbian host itself could access the network normally, but downstream devices connecting through it could not access the network normally.
First, inspect the UFW block logs:
sudo ufw logging medium sudo journalctl -k -f -o cat | grep --line-buffered 'UFW BLOCK' The following is a representative sanitized log. The IP addresses use the RFC 5737 documentation example ranges and must not be copied directly into a real network configuration:
[UFW BLOCK] IN=eth0 OUT= SRC=192.0.2.20 DST=192.0.2.254 PROTO=TCP DPT=9091 SYN [UFW BLOCK] IN=eth0 OUT= SRC=192.0.2.20 DST=192.0.2.254 PROTO=TCP DPT=22703 SYN Here, OUT= is empty and the destination is a local address, so these requests are classified as INPUT (accessing the Armbian host itself) rather than ordinary FORWARD traffic. The earlier direct suspicion of deny routed was therefore incomplete.
Next, use the following command to identify the listening processes:
sudo ss -lntup | grep -E ':(9091|22703)\b' The results show that both TCP ports are being listened on by sing-box, with one bound to the LAN IPv4 address and the other bound to the wildcard address. After allowing the corresponding inbound ports, downstream devices regained network access. It is important to emphasize that this demonstrates the relevance of port reachability to the failure, but the listening results alone do not prove that these ports are TUN ports or serve any particular function. The sing-box configuration should be checked to determine their exact purpose.
If a service is intended only for LAN use, UFW can restrict the rule to the actual LAN address and subnet. The following is merely a rule template using the RFC 5737 example subnet; it must be replaced with your actual values:
sudo ufw allow in on eth0 from 192.0.2.0/24 to 192.0.2.254 port 9091 proto tcp sudo ufw allow in on eth0 from 192.0.2.0/24 to 192.0.2.254 port 22703 proto tcp Security note: It is not recommended to execute ufw allow 22703/tcp directly without source restrictions. If the port is listening on the wildcard address, particular care should be taken to check whether public IPv6 access has been unintentionally exposed. Nor should all routed traffic be changed to be allowed by default on a long-term basis merely to restore downstream network access.
The key troubleshooting points from this addendum are: first distinguish INPUT from FORWARD using IN / OUT, then confirm the listening process, and finally allow traffic precisely based on its actual source. The UFW status page also cannot replace nft list ruleset, because sing-box’s auto_redirect creates separate nftables rules.

When running UFW and sing-box TUN simultaneously on a Linux bypass router, an easily misdiagnosed failure may occur: sing-box runs normally on the local machine, but LAN devices cannot access the Internet through the bypass router. Even if the TCP port that was blocked at the time is allowed, the problem may reappear after sing-box is restarted.
This article documents an actually observed cause and a fix pending regression validation. All examples use documentation-reserved addresses and do not correspond to a real network.
Environment and symptoms A Linux bypass router with the LAN interface eth0 and the address 192.0.2.1 (example only). A downstream client, 192.0.2.20, using the bypass router as its IPv4 gateway. The sing-box TUN interface is named tun0, with auto_route and auto_redirect enabled. UFW denies unsolicited inbound traffic by default. The key sing-box configuration is:
{ "type": "tun", "interface_name": "tun0", "auto_route": true, "auto_redirect": true } Logs during the failure are similar to:
[UFW BLOCK] IN=eth0 OUT= SRC=192.0.2.20 DST=192.0.2.1 PROTO=TCP DPT=24461 SYN DPT=24461 is only a dynamic port observed during one run, and it should not be hardcoded permanently in UFW. An empty OUT= indicates that the packet is entering the local machine’s INPUT path rather than merely traversing the FORWARD path.
Tracing NAT redirection Check the sing-box listeners:
sudo ss -lntup | grep sing-box Check nftables:
sudo nft -a list ruleset | grep -n -C 8 -E 'redirect|tproxy' In the failure scenario, rules similar to the following can be seen:
meta l4proto tcp redirect to :24461 # 内部端口不允许直接连接 tcp dport 24461 ct status ! dnat reject with tcp reset In other words, sing-box first redirects the destination TCP connection to a local listening port, and then UFW’s INPUT rules determine whether to allow it. Treating this type of traffic as ordinary FORWARD packets and allowing it will usually not eliminate the observed INPUT block.
Fix approach: Match DNAT connections rather than dynamic ports For an explicitly trusted single downstream client, you can temporarily try:
sudo iptables -I ufw-before-input 1 \ -i eth0 \ -s 192.0.2.20/32 \ -d 192.0.2.1 \ -p tcp \ -m conntrack --ctstate DNAT \ -j ACCEPT Be sure to replace the example IP address and interface with the actual values. DNAT is a valid virtual state for --ctstate; it is not valid for --ctstatus, which produces the error Bad ctstatus "DNAT".
This rule still has security boundaries: it matches qualifying DNAT TCP connections, not just connections created by sing-box. Therefore, the source and ingress interface should be restricted, and INPUT should not be allowed globally merely as a shortcut.
Validation Run the following on the downstream device:
curl -4 -v --connect-timeout 5 https://www.cloudflare.com/ Observe the rule counters and block logs on the bypass router:
sudo iptables -L ufw-before-input -n -v --line-numbers sudo journalctl -k --since '10 minutes ago' --grep='UFW BLOCK' --no-pager Only if the counters increase, Internet connectivity is restored, and things continue to work after sing-box is restarted and the internal port changes can this method be considered suitable for the current deployment.
Persistence After confirming that validation succeeded, create a backup first:
sudo cp -a /etc/ufw/before.rules /etc/ufw/before.rules.bak sudo nano /etc/ufw/before.rules In the *filter section, add the following after all chain definitions and before the existing ufw-before-input processing rules:
-A ufw-before-input -i eth0 -s 192.0.2.20/32 -d 192.0.2.1 -p tcp -m conntrack --ctstate DNAT -j ACCEPT Check and reload:
sudo iptables-restore --test < /etc/ufw/before.rules sudo ufw reload To roll back, restore the file from the backup and run sudo ufw reload. Temporary test rules can also be removed using iptables -D with exactly the same matching arguments that were used when inserting the rule.
Precautions Do not use ufw default allow routed or disable UFW entirely as a long-term solution. This approach primarily addresses INPUT blocking after IPv4 TCP redirection; it is not a universal fix for all UDP, IPv6, or WireGuard failures. Access to other explicitly configured listening ports, such as those for APIs, DNS, or SOCKS, should continue to be restricted by source according to their actual use. Both UFW and sing-box may modify nftables. If the rule match counters increase but connections still fail, also check the hook priorities of other base chains and any subsequent drop rules. References Official sing-box TUN documentation iptables-extensions: conntrack match documentation

Automatically Banning Malicious IPs on a Debian Server with CrowdSec Public-facing servers face all kinds of automated scanning every single day.
Even when you never advertise a service address, your SSH port still routinely receives login attempts against usernames like root, admin and test. Web services may get probed for paths such as .env, wp-admin and phpinfo.php.
Most of these requests come from automated scanners. They may not amount to an actual intrusion, but they generate a huge amount of pointless log noise and widen the exposed attack surface.
Relying on static firewall rules alone makes it hard to adjust the ban list dynamically based on actual attack behaviour.
That’s why I chose to try CrowdSec: identify malicious behaviour from server logs, then work with nftables to automatically ban the source of the attack.
This article records the process of deploying CrowdSec on Debian 12, and how it decides whether an IP should be banned.
1. What Is CrowdSec? CrowdSec is an open-source intrusion detection and security response system.
It analyses the logs produced by services such as SSH and web servers to detect brute-force attacks, vulnerability scanning and malicious crawlers.
Unlike a traditional static IP blacklist, CrowdSec mainly decides whether to ban based on behavioural characteristics, and it can also draw on community threat intelligence.
CrowdSec’s work splits into two parts:
Security Engine: reads the logs, identifies attacks and produces ban decisions. Remediation Component (Bouncer): carries out those ban decisions, for example by modifying firewall rules. The two are independent of each other.
In other words, installing only the CrowdSec Security Engine will not automatically block network connections.
1.1 How It Works SSH / Caddy / Nginx | v Application Logs | v CrowdSec Parser | v Detection Scenarios | v Security Alerts | v Decision Profiles | v Local API | v Firewall Bouncer | v nftables | v Block IP By decoupling log analysis from firewall enforcement, CrowdSec works just as well on a single server as it does across a fleet of machines, where a central API dispatches ban decisions to many hosts.
1.2 CrowdSec vs Fail2ban Fail2ban is a common automatic banning tool on Linux.
Both can detect SSH brute-force attempts from logs, but the design philosophies differ.
Feature CrowdSec Fail2ban SSH brute-force detection Supported Supported Web attack detection Supported Supported, usually needs a matching filter Community threat intelligence Supported Usually needs extra integration Distributed deployment Native support Usually requires your own integration Ban mechanism Bouncer Action Detection rules Parser + Scenario Filter + Jail Configuration complexity Relatively high Relatively low If all you need is to ban IPs that fail SSH logins, Fail2ban is already good enough.
If you want to protect multiple web services, SSH and other network services at once, CrowdSec’s modular architecture leaves more room to scale.
2. Deployment Environment This article uses the following environment:
Item Configuration Operating system Debian 12 Bookworm CrowdSec 1.8.x Firewall nftables Installation method APT Detection targets SSH, Caddy, Nginx Ban mechanism Firewall Bouncer I use a native installation rather than Docker.
The main reason is that CrowdSec needs to read the host’s systemd journal and, through the Bouncer, operate the system firewall. A native install avoids extra permission, network and mount configuration.
3. Installing CrowdSec 3.1 Add the Official APT Repository First install the dependencies:
sudo apt update sudo apt install -y \ debian-archive-keyring \ ca-certificates \ curl \ gnupg Create the keyring directory:
sudo install -d -m 0755 /etc/apt/keyrings Import the signing key for the CrowdSec repository:
curl -fsSL \ https://packagecloud.io/crowdsec/crowdsec/gpgkey | sudo gpg --dearmor \ -o /etc/apt/keyrings/crowdsec.gpg Add the repository:
echo \ "deb [signed-by=/etc/apt/keyrings/crowdsec.gpg] https://packagecloud.io/crowdsec/crowdsec/any any main" | sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/crowdsec.list Refresh the APT cache:
sudo apt update Check where the package comes from:
apt-cache policy crowdsec Once you’ve confirmed you’re using the official repository, install it:
sudo apt install -y crowdsec Check the version:
sudo cscli version Look at the service:
sudo systemctl status crowdsec 3.2 Install the Firewall Bouncer CrowdSec itself handles detection but does not enforce firewall bans directly.
So you need to install a Firewall Bouncer as well.
This article uses nftables:
sudo apt install -y \ crowdsec-firewall-bouncer-nftables Enable the service at boot:
sudo systemctl enable --now \ crowdsec-firewall-bouncer Check its status:
sudo systemctl status \ crowdsec-firewall-bouncer Check that the Bouncer has registered with CrowdSec:
sudo cscli bouncers list Normally you should see:
Name Valid Type firewall-bouncer true crowdsec-firewall-bouncer The name is just an example — the real one may carry an auto-generated suffix from the installation.
The Bouncer configuration file is usually located at:
/etc/crowdsec/bouncers/crowdsec-firewall-bouncer.yaml The parts worth paying attention to are:
mode: nftables api_url: http://127.0.0.1:8080/ It also contains the API key.
The APT install normally handles API registration automatically, so overwriting the entire configuration file is not recommended.
4. Configuring SSH Attack Detection SSH is one of the most common entry points for attacks against public-facing servers.
Even with password login disabled, you can still receive a large volume of invalid-username probes and public-key authentication attempts.
4.1 Install the SSH Collection The CrowdSec Hub provides predefined SSH detection rules.
Install it:
sudo cscli collections install \ crowdsecurity/sshd View it:
sudo cscli collections list A Collection is a set of Parsers and Scenarios, where:
The Parser is responsible for understanding SSH logs. The Scenario is responsible for deciding whether something counts as an attack. 4.2 Configure journald Debian 12 uses systemd by default, so SSH logs can be read straight from journald.
Check first:
sudo journalctl -u ssh.service \ -n 20 --no-pager If you can see SSH login records, you can configure CrowdSec to read the matching logs.
Create the file:
/etc/crowdsec/acquis.d/ssh.yaml Write:
source: journalctl journalctl_filter: - "_SYSTEMD_UNIT=ssh.service" labels: type: syslog Two details matter here.
First, journalctl_filter must match the actual log fields.
Second, type: syslog tells CrowdSec to use the corresponding log parsing pipeline — it should not be casually changed to sshd.
If the auto-discovered log source installed at setup time already covers SSH, avoid collecting the same data twice.
Validate the configuration:
sudo crowdsec -t Restart the service:
sudo systemctl restart crowdsec Check acquisition:
sudo cscli metrics show acquisition Once new SSH log events appear, the corresponding source should show up in the acquisition metrics.
4.3 Verify SSH Log Parsing You can use cscli explain to test the log parser.
The example below uses the documentation-reserved IP, so it doesn’t expose a real attack source:
sudo cscli explain \ --log 'Oct 19 18:48:40 server sshd[1234]: Invalid user test from 203.0.113.10 port 51878' \ --type syslog If parsing succeeds, you should see the corresponding syslog and SSH parsing pipeline.
Note: cscli explain is a log-parsing diagnostic tool — a single test record like this will not get an IP banned.
5. Configuring Caddy Log Detection Besides SSH, CrowdSec can also identify malicious HTTP requests from a reverse proxy’s access logs.
Caddy is used as the example here.
5.1 Install the Caddy Collection sudo cscli collections install \ crowdsecurity/caddy If you also run Nginx, install this as well:
sudo cscli collections install \ crowdsecurity/nginx 5.2 Configure Log Acquisition Suppose Caddy’s access logs are stored in:
/var/log/caddy/ and use JSON format.
Create:
/etc/crowdsec/acquis.d/caddy.yaml Contents:
filenames: - /var/log/caddy/*.log labels: type: caddy Restart CrowdSec:
sudo crowdsec -t sudo systemctl restart crowdsec Check:
sudo cscli metrics show acquisition If it shows logs being read and parsed, the acquisitor and the parser are working.
That said, it does not mean malicious requests have been detected yet.
5.3 How Does CrowdSec Judge HTTP Attacks? CrowdSec judges based on different Scenarios, asking questions such as:
Whether sensitive files are being accessed repeatedly in a row. Whether a large number of non-existent paths are being probed. Whether known vulnerability-probing behaviour is present. Whether the HTTP request rate is abnormal. Whether the request matches the behaviour signature of known malicious HTTP clients. For example, requests to these paths:
/.env /wp-admin/ /phpinfo.php /.git/config These paths show up in automated scans all the time.
But a single visit does not necessarily trigger a ban.
CrowdSec evaluates the rules of the specific Scenario, so that normal traffic isn’t misjudged as an attack.
6. When Does CrowdSec Actually Ban an IP? This is the single most important thing to understand when using CrowdSec.
CrowdSec does not ban an IP the moment it sees one failed SSH login. It generates alerts and ban decisions once the behaviour meets a Scenario’s detection conditions.
6.1 The Leaky Bucket Algorithm Many CrowdSec Scenarios use the Leaky Bucket algorithm.
You can think of each IP as an individual bucket:
Every qualifying attack event adds one unit to the bucket. The bucket leaks continuously at a configured rate. If events accumulate faster than they leak, the bucket overflows and an attack alert is triggered. For example, a hypothetical rule:
type: leaky capacity: 5 leakspeed: "10s" This means:
The bucket has a capacity of 5. One event leaks out every 10 seconds. An overflow is triggered when accumulated events exceed the capacity. If an attacker keeps trying to log in over a short period, a ban may be triggered.
If attempts happen only once every few minutes, the events may have leaked away before reaching the threshold.
This is also why some IPs that scanned through multiple usernames in a row were not banned immediately.
6.2 Inspect the Real Detection Thresholds Don’t guess at CrowdSec’s default thresholds from memory.
Different Scenarios, Hub versions and local custom rules may use different parameters.
Inspect the SSH brute-force rule:
sudo cscli scenarios inspect \ crowdsecurity/ssh-bf You can also read the installed rule file directly:
cat /etc/crowdsec/scenarios/ssh-bf.yaml Focus on:
capacity: leakspeed: groupby: distinct: Where:
capacity determines the bucket size. leakspeed determines how fast events decay. groupby usually groups by source IP. distinct prevents repeated events from being counted over and over. So CrowdSec should not be reduced to “5 failures within 10 minutes and you get banned.”
The real trigger condition is defined by the Scenario’s complete rule set.
6.3 How Long Does the Ban Last? After producing an Alert, CrowdSec uses a Profile to decide whether to generate a ban Decision.
Check it:
cat /etc/crowdsec/profiles.yaml A common IP ban policy looks like this:
name: default_ip_remediation filters: - Alert.Remediation == true && Alert.GetScope() == "Ip" decisions: - type: ban duration: 4h on_success: break Where:
duration: 4h means the ban lasts 4 hours.
The Profile that is actually installed may contain other conditions or policies, so check the full configuration before editing — and avoid defining a rule with the same name twice.
6.4 From Alert to an Actual Ban Even after a Scenario has fired, several further conditions must be met:
The detection scenario produces an Alert. The Profile converts the Alert into a Decision. The Firewall Bouncer pulls the Decision. nftables adds the source IP to the ban set. An actual firewall rule matches that source IP. If any one of these steps fails, you can end up in a situation where CrowdSec shows attack alerts but the network connections are not actually blocked.
7. Verifying That Automatic Bans Work A successful installation does not mean the whole ban chain has been verified.
It makes sense to split this into two parts: first verify firewall enforcement, then verify attack detection.
7.1 Check the Bouncer sudo cscli bouncers list Confirm that:
The Bouncer is registered. API authentication is valid. It has been pulling Decisions recently. 7.2 Create a Test Ban Using an RFC 5737 documentation example IP:
sudo cscli decisions add \ --ip 203.0.113.10 \ --type ban \ --duration 5m \ --reason manual-test List the decisions:
sudo cscli decisions list Then check nftables:
sudo nft list ruleset | grep -i crowdsec Confirm that the banned IP has entered the corresponding set:
sudo nft list ruleset | grep '203.0.113.10' If you can see the test IP, and the set is referenced by an effective firewall rule, the Bouncer has synced the ban decision to the firewall.
Release it once the test is done:
sudo cscli decisions delete \ --ip 203.0.113.10 Note that 203.0.113.10 is a documentation test address: it’s fine for verifying decision sync, but not for testing whether a real network connection gets blocked.
7.3 Look at Real Attack Alerts sudo cscli alerts list View the ban decisions:
sudo cscli decisions list View Scenario metrics:
sudo cscli metrics show scenarios If a Scenario’s Overflow counter increases, the attack detection rule has fired.
But whether a ban was actually produced has to be judged together with the Profile, Simulation and Decision.
Check the Simulation status:
sudo cscli simulation status If a Scenario is in simulation mode, it may only produce detection results without enforcing the ban.
7.4 Avoid Locking Out Your Own Management IP When testing bans on a public-facing server, the most important thing is not to lock out your only way in.
Recommendations:
Have the cloud provider’s console ready in advance. Never directly ban the egress IP of your current SSH client. Set up the necessary AllowList for trusted, fixed management addresses. Confirm nftables rule priority before changing any policy. Use another controlled device for real connection tests. 8. Does CrowdSec Look at Old Logs? By default, CrowdSec mainly focuses on real-time log analysis, and it does not guarantee that it will automatically scan all historical logs from before the installation at startup.
For example, before CrowdSec was deployed, the SSH log may already contain several hundred failed login attempts.
Those events will not all turn into current ban decisions merely because CrowdSec was installed.
8.1 Normal Operation Situation Handling Newly generated SSH logs Real-time detection Newly generated Caddy logs Real-time detection Historical logs from before installation Usually not backfilled automatically Need to re-analyse old logs Use Replay Mode The actual starting point for reading may still depend on the data source and its configuration.
8.2 Export Historical SSH Logs For example, export the past 24 hours:
sudo journalctl -u ssh.service \ --since "24 hours ago" \ --output=short \ --no-pager \ > /tmp/ssh-history.log CrowdSec can analyse existing log files through Replay Mode.
It replays events according to the original timestamps in the log, and judges whether the detection threshold was reached at that time.
Be aware, however, that Replay may submit alerts to the API, so you shouldn’t casually replay large amounts of historical attack logs directly on a production environment.
A safer approach is to use a separate configuration and a test environment, so that real ban decisions aren’t affected.
Official documentation:
https://docs.crowdsec.net/u/user_guides/replay_mode/
9. Day-to-Day Management CrowdSec provides the cscli command-line tool, and most routine maintenance can be done from the terminal.
9.1 Check Service Status systemctl status crowdsec systemctl status crowdsec-firewall-bouncer 9.2 Check Log Acquisition sudo cscli metrics show acquisition 9.3 Check Parser Metrics sudo cscli metrics show parsers 9.4 Check Scenario Metrics sudo cscli metrics show scenarios 9.5 View Banned IPs sudo cscli decisions list 9.6 Ban Manually sudo cscli decisions add \ --ip 203.0.113.10 \ --duration 4h \ --reason manual-ban 9.7 Unban Manually sudo cscli decisions delete \ --ip 203.0.113.10 9.8 View CrowdSec Logs sudo journalctl -u crowdsec -f View the Bouncer logs:
sudo journalctl \ -u crowdsec-firewall-bouncer -f 9.9 Update the Rules Rules from the CrowdSec Hub can be updated independently:
sudo cscli hub update sudo cscli hub upgrade Updating detection rules is not the same as upgrading the CrowdSec software itself. The software update is still managed through APT.
10. Frequently Asked Questions CrowdSec Is Running but Nothing Is Being Banned First check log acquisition:
sudo cscli metrics show acquisition Then check the parsers:
sudo cscli metrics show parsers Then check:
sudo cscli metrics show scenarios sudo cscli alerts list sudo cscli decisions list Finally check the Bouncer and nftables:
sudo cscli bouncers list sudo nft list ruleset The correct troubleshooting order is:
Log Acquisition ↓ Parser ↓ Scenario ↓ Alert ↓ Decision ↓ Bouncer ↓ Firewall Don’t rush to change the ban thresholds before you’ve confirmed that the logs are actually being read.
Why Are There Lots of Attack Logs but No Bans? Because the number of log lines isn’t the same as the number of events that meet the detection conditions.
Some logs may not have been parsed correctly, and some may simply not match the Scenario’s filter.
Also, even if the same IP fails to log in many times, if the interval between two events is long enough, the Leaky Bucket may never overflow.
It Says I’ve Been Banned, but I Can Still Get In Possible causes include:
The Bouncer hasn’t synced the Decision yet. The nftables rule isn’t hooked into the point where traffic actually passes. The firewall rules are in the wrong order. IPv4 and IPv6 aren’t both covered. The traffic actually goes through a reverse proxy, so the IP in the log isn’t the real client address. The blocked connection and the connection you’re testing with come from different sources. So cscli decisions list only proves that CrowdSec produced a decision — on its own it cannot prove that the network layer blocked the traffic.
Does CrowdSec Automatically Unban? Yes.
Once a ban Decision expires, the Bouncer should sync the firewall set and remove the corresponding IP.
However, if the same IP is also blocked by some other firewall rule, CrowdSec unbanning it will not automatically remove those independent rules.
11. Conclusion The real value of CrowdSec isn’t just automatic IP banning — it’s splitting log parsing, behaviour detection and ban enforcement into independent components.
That lets you start from the most basic SSH brute-force protection and expand step by step to web services, reverse proxies and centralised multi-server protection.
In a real deployment, there are three things worth understanding:
First, CrowdSec does not ban based on a fixed number of failures. It uses Scenarios to judge whether behaviour is abnormal, and many rules use the Leaky Bucket algorithm, so both the frequency and the duration of an attack affect the detection result.
Second, successful detection is not the same as a successful ban. Alerts, Decisions, Bouncers and firewall rules are different stages — when troubleshooting, confirm them layer by layer.
Third, CrowdSec suits continuous monitoring of newly generated security events. If you need to analyse historical attacks, Replay Mode is available, but you should avoid letting historical alerts accidentally affect production bans.
For servers already running Debian, systemd, Caddy or Nginx, CrowdSec together with nftables is an automated security-protection option worth considering.
It cannot replace timely software updates, secure configuration, SSH public-key authentication and the principle of least privilege — but it can cut down a large volume of repetitive automated scanning and brute-force requests.
References CrowdSec Official Website CrowdSec Official Documentation Linux Installation Guide Firewall Bouncer How Scenarios Detect Replay Mode CrowdSec GitHub
summary:
Automatically Banning Malicious IPs on a Debian Server with CrowdSec

Public-facing servers face all kinds of automated scanning every single day.

Even when you never advertise a service address, your SSH port still routinely receives login attempts against usernames like root, admin and test. Web services may get probed for paths such as .env, wp-admin and phpinfo.php.

Most of these requests come from automated scanners. They may not amount to an actual intrusion, but they generate a huge amount of pointless log noise and widen the exposed attack surface.
